---
title: Neutron stars and pulsars
lang: en
free: true
---
A neutron star is the ultra-dense remnant left behind after a massive star explodes as a supernova. With a mass comparable to the Sun packed into a sphere roughly 20 kilometres across, neutron stars are the densest objects astronomers can directly observe. A teaspoon of their material would weigh roughly a billion tonnes on Earth. The interior is so compressed that protons and electrons merge into neutrons, giving the object its name.

Neutron stars form when a stellar core between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses survives the supernova blast. Below that threshold, a white dwarf forms; above it, collapse continues all the way to a black hole.

## Pulsars: cosmic lighthouses

Many neutron stars rotate rapidly and emit beams of radio waves or X-rays from their magnetic poles. When the beam sweeps past Earth, observers receive a regular pulse — hence the name pulsar. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times per second, making them extraordinarily stable natural clocks more precise than most atomic clocks on Earth.

## Magnetars and gravitational laboratories

A subset of neutron stars, called magnetars, possess magnetic fields a trillion times stronger than Earth's. Sudden shifts in a magnetar's crust release enormous bursts of gamma-ray energy. More broadly, neutron stars serve as natural laboratories for testing physics at extremes of density and gravity impossible to replicate on Earth.
